Anchor: '...who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime.'

The source calls Walter a painter and describes his practice ('He paints on ripped cardboard and fading paper; he depicts rainbows and stars...'), and attributes 'his work' and 'his weird little paintings' to him. Combined with 'thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime', authorship is licensed rather than merely collection.

Anchors: George 'never showed her work publicly in her lifetime, and was only discovered after her death in 2013'; Walter 'died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings'. Both are placed outside their own lifetimes by the source.
Characterising the tone the word carries in the review (pleasure of the find, a story surfacing) is a reading of the source's Columbo and hidden-stories framing, not an added fact.

Judgement that the word fits the visitor's case, resting on 'You can't walk into a gallery without learning about... you've never heard of.' Evaluative, adds nothing about the world.
The article drawing the consequence of two grounded facts (never shown in lifetime, discovered after death). Reasoning, not new world-state content.
